candidates.title: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence: Big Data, Processors and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This chapter reviews the interdependencies among AI-specialized microprocessors, big data ecosystems, and large-scale foundation models, including large language models (LLMs) and large multimodal models (LMMs). The primary objective is to analyze how the convergence of data availability, algorithmic advancements, and hardware innovation has reshaped the artificial intelligence (AI) landscape and accelerated the development of generative AI systems. Drawing on industry reports, technical documentation, and recent literature published between 2024 and 2025, this study examines three critical dimensions: (i) the evolution of processing architectures from general-purpose CPUs to specialized accelerators such as GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, and emerging paradigms (i.e., neuromorphic and photonic computing), (ii) the role of large-scale and multimodal big data in enabling foundation model training, and (iii) the growing energy consumption and sustainability challenges associated with large AI systems. In addition, national and global semiconductor strategies, including investments in exascale supercomputing and sovereign AI infrastructures, are analyzed to understand geopolitical and technological dynamics. The findings highlight three key insights. First, the co-evolution of big data, processors, and model architectures forms the foundational driver of modern AI capabilities. Second, the rapid scaling of LLMs and LMMs has significantly increased computational and energy demands, making hardware efficiency and infrastructure design critical bottlenecks. Third, global competition in semiconductor technologies and AI infrastructure is intensifying, with nations prioritizing technological sovereignty and secure access to advanced computing resources. In conclusion, the future of AI depends on a balanced integration of scalable data ecosystems, energy-efficient hardware, and advanced model architectures. Sustainable and secure AI development will require coordinated efforts in hardware–software co-design, algorithmic optimization, renewable energy integration, and policy-driven governance to ensure responsible and inclusive technological progress. Modern AI relies on three key interconnected pillars: LLMs for advanced language processing, LMMs for handling diverse data types (i.e., text, images, audio, video) beyond language alone, and AI-specialized microprocessors (i.e., GPUs, TPUs, custom accelerators) that supply the massive computational power needed for training and running these models efficiently. Together, these enable foundation models capable of broad, generalized learning and real-world applications while posing significant challenges in energy use, scalability, and deployment as observed in research and industry trends from 2024–2025.

candidates.title: Transforming Research Management and Knowledge Creation With Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed academic research and institutional operations. Major LLMs, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, are now integrated into educational institutions at research and administrative levels. These LLMs go beyond summarizing text or polishing emails to include personalized learning, automated content creation, decision-making, and pedagogical integration. This chapter investigates the evolving role of LLMs in transforming the research landscape, particularly in academic writing, research management, pedagogy, evaluation, and ethical consideration. The research method is based on a systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA protocols, supported by bibliometric analysis and keyword-based thematic analysis of peer-reviewed articles from Web of Science and Scopus databases (2020–2025). Results revealed the existence of five major themes, namely academic writing and content generation, research evaluation, pedagogical integration, model comparison, and ethical considerations. The study highlights a sharp increase in publications since ChatGPT’s emergence, with thematic shifts toward education-related applications. Heatmaps across Scopus and WoS demonstrated significant trends toward real-world educational applications. However, ethical concerns showed strong growth, reflecting academic integrity issues. The keyword co-occurrence analysis also showed a dynamic research landscape with strong thematic ties to ethics, academic writing, teaching, and educational innovation. The overlay visualizations further illustrated the temporal evolution of topics from foundational concepts toward technology adoption, user experience, and collaborative learning. This chapter concludes by suggesting some recommendations to guide institutional policy and future research, ensuring an effective integration of LLMs in academic settings.

candidates.title: Decoupled visual processing: Efficient multimodal adaptation via modality-specific transformer substitution
candidates.abstract: Abstract Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities by integrating visual and textual understanding within a unified transformer architecture. However, fine-tuning all parameters of these models for visual instruction tuning is computationally expensive and often unnecessary, as the representation requirements for visual and textual tokens diverge significantly in the deeper layers of the network. In this paper, we propose decoupled visual processing (DVP), an efficient training framework that replaces the upper decoder layers of a pretrained LLM with a lightweight, independently trainable single transformer block dedicated exclusively to visual token processing. Specifically, after shared processing through the first half of the decoder layers, visual and textual tokens are split: visual tokens are routed through a newly initialized single transformer block while textual tokens continue through the original frozen decoder layers. The two streams are then concatenated before the language modeling head. During training, only the single transformer block is updated, dramatically reducing the number of trainable parameters. Experiments on the LLaVA-1.5 framework demonstrate that DVP achieves competitive performance on MME, POPE, and ChartQA benchmarks while training only a fraction of the total parameters, suggesting that visual representations in MLLMs can be effectively learned through a decoupled, parameter-efficient pathway.

candidates.title: Towards Enhancing Learning Outcomes in Higher Education: Proposing a Conceptual Model of Personalized AI Tutoring Systems
candidates.abstract: Abstract The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) drives the potential of enhancing learning experiences and personalizing the learning process in higher education. The large language models (LLMs) evolution of generative AI further steers the potential of developing personalized AI tutoring systems (PAITS) for achieving higher learning outcomes in higher education. PAITS can act as a personalized tutor to provide immediate support and guidance to learners’ needs, learning abilities and preferences for progressive, adaptive and active learning. However, developing a fully functioning PAITS requires to be equipped with the core features and the model/framework to structure the core features effectively that are largely unexplored. Therefore, this study aims to identify the core features of PAITS and propose a conceptual model equipped with the core features of PAITS towards enhancing learning outcomes in higher education. The study follows a qualitative research approach to point out the key features/elements of PAITS through the content analysis of state-of-the-art scholarly articles. The findings of this study can be useful for developing intelligent systems for achieving higher learning outcomes in higher education. Also, it can be considered as a reference point and guidance for further study on the subject. Both practitioners and relevant stakeholders in the context of higher education can avail benefits from the outcomes of this study.

candidates.title: A Textile Standardization Large Language Model Integrating LoRA Fine-Tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Intelligent question answering for textile standards requires accurate domain understanding, clause retrieval, and evidence-grounded generation, yet general-purpose large language models often lack sufficient domain adaptation and factual support. This study proposes a textile-standard question-answering framework that integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning with multidimensional retrieval-augmented generation (MDRAG). Based on 7017 domestic and international textile standards, we constructed a structured knowledge resource containing 121,166 annotated domain elements and a task-specific dataset of 2000 question–answer pairs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, and GLM-4-9B were evaluated under three primary settings: Baseline, Baseline+LoRA, and Baseline+LoRA+MDRAG. A separate comparison with conventional RAG was conducted to assess the additional benefit of multidimensional retrieval over single-path retrieval. Among the primary settings, Qwen3.5-9B-Base with LoRA+MDRAG achieved the highest overall performance, with a cosine similarity of 0.624, a BLEU score of 0.283, and an expert-based overall score of 24.4. These findings support the use of lightweight domain adaptation together with multidimensional structured knowledge retrieval for textile-standard question answering.

candidates.title: Metric-dependent evaluation of a retrieval-augmented large language model workflow for oral squamous cell carcinoma treatment planning: a retrospective study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but open-ended treatment planning poses a measurement problem: a clinically defensible recommendation may differ from a historical plan, and different automated metrics may reward different properties of the same output. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) may improve evidence grounding, but its contribution cannot be inferred without controlled ablation. We evaluated how four archived RAG-enabled LLM configurations agreed with clinician treatment plans for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and whether apparent model ranking depended on the evaluation method. Methods This single-center retrospective evaluation used the same 100-case OSCC study set for four archived configurations (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Doubao, and Qwen). Generated treatment plans were compared with archived clinician plans using a DeepSeek-based LLM-judge score, m3e-base embedding cosine similarity, ROUGE-1 recall, and an archived blinded five-physician rating protocol. Cohort descriptors were audited from the de-identified case register. Because complete case-level metric arrays and the case-by-rater matrix were not retained, model comparisons were summarized descriptively and no unsupported paired inference was reconstructed. Results The cohort had a mean age of 59.5 years (SD 13.6); 65% of cases were male and 69% were source-coded N0. Model ordering differed by automated metric: Qwen had the highest mean LLM-judge score (0.809; DeepSeek-R1, 0.807), Doubao had the highest mean embedding similarity (0.8489), and Claude had the highest mean ROUGE-1 recall (0.2729). No configuration was uniformly best. The archived clinician-rating summary showed a different descriptive pattern, but formal inter-rater reliability and paired model comparisons could not be recomputed from the available archive. Conclusions In this retrospective OSCC treatment-planning evaluation, apparent model performance was inseparable from the reference standard and evaluation method. The findings support feasibility of the combined RAG-enabled workflow and demonstrate the limitations of selecting a clinical LLM from a single aggregate metric; they do not establish clinical equivalence, autonomous safety, patient benefit, or a causal advantage of RAG. Future validation should use time-aligned evidence, locked system configurations, independent clinical adjudication, paired case-level analyses, severity-weighted safety assessment, controlled RAG ablation, and clinician-in-the-loop prospective evaluation.

candidates.title: From Retrieval to Recognition:Knowledge-Enhanced Post-training of Time Series Foundation Models for Classification
candidates.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have achieved notable progress in classification tasks through large-scale pretraining. However, their post-training practice mainly focuses on implicit parameter fine-tuning, where task-relevant information is entangled with abundant irrelevant knowledge in vast parameter spaces. This may hinder TSFMs from precisely activating useful knowledge for downstream classification. To this end, we propose Retrieval-to-Recognition (R2R), a plug-and-play post-training paradigm that adapts pretrained TSFMs to time series classification. Rather than pretraining a new foundation model, R2R improves how existing TSFMs are post-trained: it introduces a decoupled query encoder to extract discriminative patterns and retrieve instance-level numerical knowledge from a constructed knowledge base. The retrieved explicit knowledge is then fused with the TSFM's implicit parametric embeddings, enabling joint knowledge transfer at both the parameter and feature levels. In this way, R2R allows TSFMs to recall task-relevant patterns learned during pretraining, improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in downstream classification transfer. Experiments on 158 time series datasets show that R2R consistently improves the classification performance of state-of-the-art TSFMs. Ablation and knowledge-enhanced studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

candidates.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
candidates.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

candidates.title: Optimizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Privacy-Preserving Local Cognitive Agents Using Small Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled advanced language understanding, knowledge retrieval, reasoning, and intelligent decision-making. However, cloud-centric language processing introduces concerns related to data privacy, network dependency, communication latency, and computational cost. Small Language Models (SLMs) provide a promising alternative for local inference, but their limited computational capacity and reduced contextual knowledge create additional challenges for knowledge-intensive applications. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by combining language generation with externally retrieved knowledge. Nevertheless, conventional RAG pipelines are not necessarily optimized for resource-constrained local SLM deployment. Embedding selection, document chunking, vector indexing, retrieval depth, context construction, and inference latency can significantly influence the overall performance of a local RAG system. This research proposes and implements an optimization-oriented RAG framework, FRIDAY (Fast Retrieval-Integrated Digital Assistant for You), for privacy-preserving local cognitive agents using Small Language Models. The methodology investigates embedding optimization, document preprocessing, semantic retrieval, vector database indexing, retrieval parameter selection, context optimization, privacy- aware guardrails, and local SLM inference. A working prototype was implemented and evaluated using retrieval accuracy, embedding and retrieval latency, ingestion throughput, similarity quality, and privacy-policy enforcement. The results establish a quantitative baseline that demonstrates the feasibility of a fully local, privacy-preserving RAG pipeline and identifies the specific components that benefit most from further optimization.

candidates.title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.

candidates.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.

candidates.title: EpiLens: Lightweight RAG for Epidemiological Knowledge Acquisition
candidates.abstract: To prepare for future outbreaks, researchers need to know what studies have been done and what data they use. Mapping a large literature by hand is slow, while large language models alone can misstate or conflate sources. We present EpiLens, a lightweight, open-source retrieval-augmented generation package that applies a fixed retrieval template and output schema to every paper in a corpus and links outputs to source passages. We build a corpus of 2,297 papers from the sources of a multi-pathogen parameter study and evaluate EpiLens's paper-classification workflow against 214 manually labelled papers. Without task-specific training data, the classifier matches or exceeds the tested supervised and zero-shot baselines across four tasks. The study's early extraction sheets cite published sources for 327 estimates. We link each estimate to a cited document or to corpus studies included by a review. Then, we use the classifier's labels to compare the papers associated with different parameters and pathogens. EpiLens labels more papers linked to reproduction numbers than fatality risks as model-based (54% versus 22%, compared with 62% versus 24% in the manual labels). The gap is consistent with the frequent use of transmission models to estimate reproduction numbers and persists within each of five pathogens compared. Beyond the contrast between parameters, the model-based share of papers linked to incubation-period estimates differs by pathogen: 55% for SARS-CoV-2 versus 6% for mpox.

candidates.title: Traditional Machine Learning versus Large Language Models for Predicting Ship Turnaround Times at Brazilian Ports
candidates.abstract: Predicting ship turnaround time at ports is an operationally valuable regression problem on heterogeneous, text-rich tabular data. We ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can match purpose-built Machine Learning (ML) on this task, using a leakage-controlled pipeline over seven years of Brazilian (ANTAQ) data. On a fixed 200-berthing test set, with 20 seeds and seed-paired statistics (Wilcoxon, Cohen’s d), we compare five families that read the same cases: classical ML on engineered tabular features plus multilingual sentence embeddings; frontier LLMs (Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3) prompted zero-, 5and 20-shot; a small generative LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B) fine-tuned on 100–6000 serialized records; an encoder with a regression head fine-tuned on 100–12000 records; and a tabular foundation model (TabFM) reading the raw table in-context. Tuned XGBoost attains R2 ≈ 0.73. Every prompted configuration stays at R2 ≤ 0 and in-context examples do not help; generative fine-tuning barely clears zero, reaching only R2 ≈ 0.10 at 6000 examples. The encoder is the only text regime to rise substantially above R2 = 0, reaching ≈ 0.43 at 12000 examples yet still trailing all ML. In contrast, TabFM, with no task training, matches or beats a data-matched XGBoost at every budget (100–6000; R2 up to ≈ 0.60), leading the low-data regime, though full-data XGBoost still wins and TabFM is far costlier at inference. The predictive signal is tabular, not textual: text-only LLMs miss it, whereas a tabular foundation model recovers it in-context and engineered boosting wins at scale.

candidates.title: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for Tülu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.

candidates.title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but an engineer has to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. This paper presents a method for application-specific capability profiling of LLMs and its realization as a containerized testbed. The method treats each application as a unit of extension: an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation-grounded chatbot or an enterprise-support automation agent runs in its own container behind a small contract, brings its own dataset, evaluator and owned attributes, and is onboarded together with its dashboards. Measurements accumulate in a versioned, sparse metamodel of every model. The method separates the model under test from judges and agents, freezes and hashes plans, refuses to compare values from different contexts, diagnoses the instrument before the system, and applies a null-agent check and a noise rule whose operating characteristics are quantified by simulation. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choices produced larger differences on selected observable outcomes than framework choices, although the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of these factors. The experiments also show that instruction tuning is deployment-specific and that system-reported success can exceed independently observed success: of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct. These measurements establish application-specific observations, not a universal model ranking.

candidates.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

candidates.title: A retrieval-augmented multi-stage prompting framework for legal analysis in the Indian judicial system
candidates.abstract: The aim of this endeavor was to create an Artificial Intelligence (AI) based legal researcher that utilizes a multi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methodology to solve the challenges of finding and comprehending pertinent legal information in the documents. The traditional methods for finding legal documents will usually yield very few results that are useful to someone without a law degree. This new system uses semantic search, keyword retrieval and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning methods to improve the legal research process. The submitted query will be transformed into a vector embedding while simultaneously being classified into the appropriate category for retrieval. Once the query is classified, the system will use a hybrid retrieval mechanism to find the most relevant legal document based on both BM25 (Best Matching 25) and FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) search algorithms and will combine these results using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) in order to determine the best results. Later, it will be processed through LLM models to produce formatted (structured) answers to the query in accordance with the relevant legal citation. The overall performance of the proposed system demonstrates improved answer relevancy, reliability and contextual accuracy, thereby making it an effective tool for legal research and assistance. LLaMA-3.3-70B achieved the highest scores in Answer Relevancy (0.91) and Faithfulness (0.92), proving its ability to generate accurate, intent aligned, and evidence-grounded legal responses with minimal hallucination. Gemini-2.0-Flash showed higher Context Recall (0.78), indicating strong retrieval capability, while Mistral-Large excelled in BLEU (0.769) and semantic similarity, highlighting fluent text generation but weaker evidence grounding.

candidates.title: Towards More Granular Reasoning: Mapping the DSA Transparency Database Taxonomy to Platform Terms and Conditions Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Article 24(5) of the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires providers of online platforms to submit every content moderation decision they make, with a corresponding Statement of Reasons (SoR), to the DSA Transparency Database (DSA-TDB). Such decisions are classified against seventeen high-level attribute categories that categorize the primary reason for the moderation decision. Because over 99.8% of statements cite a violation of the provider's own terms and conditions rather than a legal provision, the database is overwhelmingly a record of contractual enforcement using catch-all reporting; however, whether its categories actually describe those contractual rules well has not been examined. In this paper, we map the terms and conditions (T&C) of 31 designated online services against the DSA-TDB's high-level category taxonomy using a few-shot GPT-4.1 classifier over 447 policy documents. The analysis concerns how T&C rules are represented in the taxonomy, not how they are enforced. Two findings emerge. First, high-level category applicability varies sharply by service type: unsafe products account for 17.5% of e-commerce assignments and 0.2% of adult-platform assignments, and negative effects on civic discourse reaches 9.9% within the Meta family but is absent from adult platforms, Booking.com, and Wikipedia. Second, the categories have notable overlap among sub-category specifications, which makes assigning a single high-level category to a decision difficult. We argue that catch-all reporting is plausibly in part a consequence of the DSA-TDB's schema and attribute design, and recommend a schema that is differentiated by service type with more mandatory attributes derived inductively from platform governance language.

candidates.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.

candidates.title: Tail Smoothing and Cross-Lingual Volatility: Evaluating Estimative Uncertainty in Large Language Models for Brazilian Portuguese
candidates.abstract: This study evaluates how LLMs interpret Words of Estimative Probability (WEPs) in Brazilian Portuguese compared to English. We translated an English benchmark and compared multilingual models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Flash) against a region-specific model (Sabiá 4). Our findings reveal a “tail smoothing” phenomenon, where models systematically compress extreme probabilities. Notably, while Gemini 3 Flash demonstrated remarkable cross-lingual stability, GPT-5.1 exhibited significant calibration degradation. Counterintuitively, when measured against the English human baseline, Sabiá 4 displayed the most aggressive distribution compression. These results suggest a complex dynamic: either linguistic fine-tuning does not ensure alignment, or it actively captures a culturally specific pragmatic ambiguity in Brazilian Portuguese. This exposes the vulnerabilities and nuances of deploying deploying LLMs in nuanced semantic tasks in Brazilian Portuguese.

candidates.title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1

candidates.title: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: Enhancing LLM Agents for Automated Fact-Checking with Human Expert Skills
candidates.abstract: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems powered by large language model (LLM) agents still face challenges in evidence retrieval and claim verification. Existing approaches improve their capabilities through computationally costly post-training or human-in-the-loop feedback that is difficult to scale. To transfer professional fact-checking expertise to LLM agents efficiently, we distill publicly available guidelines published by Agence France-Presse (AFP) Fact Check into a reusable, modular Professional Fact-Checking Skill (PFC-Skill). We then present SkillCheck, the first AFC system that gives LLM agents dynamic access to PFC-Skill to guide evidence retrieval and claim verification at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SkillCheck improves upon skill-free DEFAME baselines across multiple LLM backbones, with gains of 2.2--4.8 pp. in Accuracy and 1.5--6.3 pp. in Macro-F1 on the AVeriTeC benchmark. Notably, SkillCheck with GPT-4o-Mini exceeds DEFAME with GPT-4o by 3.4 pp. in Accuracy while cutting inference cost by roughly 61%. The performance gains also extend to open-web retrieval. Ablations show that incorporating the skill during evidence retrieval provides most of the gains, while incorporation into both stages yields the best overall performance. Case studies show that PFC-Skill enables more targeted search and closer scrutiny of evidence. To conclude, our work shows that LLM agents can "stand on the shoulders of giants" by drawing on the best practices of professional fact-checkers, substantially enhancing AFC performance without extra training or continuous human supervision.

candidates.title: Sentiment Classification of Saudi Stock Market Tweets: Lexicon-Based Weak Supervision, Classical Machine Learning, and Zero-Shot Open-Source Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Social media platforms have become a rich, real-time source of investor opinion, yet Arabic-language financial text remains under-studied, and much applied work validates classifiers against labels produced by the very rules they later learn to imitate. This study examines sentiment classification of 1,000 Arabic tweets about companies listed on the Saudi Exchange (Tadawul), issued by 41 accounts. Using a domain lexicon of 180 financial terms, tweets were assigned positive, negative or neutral labels, and four classical models (Multinomial Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and a linear Support Vector Machine) were trained on TF-IDF features. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation the linear SVM reproduced the lexicon labels with an accuracy of 0.861 and a macro-F1 of 0.819, whereas Naïve Bayes reached only 0.446 macro-F1. We then added a zero-shot open-source large language model (LLM), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run locally with 4-bit quantisation and no task-specific training. Its agreement with the lexicon labels was low (accuracy 0.376, macro-F1 0.401, Cohen’s κ = 0.19), driven by a strong tendency to label lexicon-neutral tweets, such as dividend declarations and earnings announcements, as positive. A diagnostic analysis showed that this disagreement reflects, to a large extent, weaknesses in the lexicon labels: the lexicon terms were not subjected to the same orthographic normalisation as the tweets, so only 42.4% of tweets matched any term; after correcting this, the match rate rose to 67.8%, 30% of labels changed, and LLM–lexicon agreement rose to 57.5% (κ = 0.31). We conclude that high accuracy against rule-derived labels demonstrates label reproduction rather than sentiment understanding, that zero-shot LLMs offer a label-free, domain-aware alternative whose outputs differ systematically from lexicon rules, and that a human-annotated reference set is indispensable for establishing which is correct. We release the pipeline, prompt and an annotation protocol to support such validation.

candidates.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
candidates.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.

candidates.title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.

candidates.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
candidates.abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

candidates.title: Modeling VIM Concepts Using Large Language Models: An LLM White-Box Study on Metrological Descriptions
candidates.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs), specifically GPT-4, can analyze, explain, and enrich concepts in the International Vocabulary of Metrology (VIM). It uses a white-box approach, in which “white-box” qualifies the input, which is fully known and traceable to a validated normative source, while the model itself remains opaque: the material supplied consisted only of VIM definitions and graphical representations of the relationships between VIM terms, together with the relationship types of the informative Annex A of the VIM. The outputs were analyzed qualitatively by structured expert cross-review against three criteria: fidelity to VIM concepts, terminological consistency, and explanatory quality. Across the seven cases examined (four topology diagrams and three VIM concepts), GPT-4 generated structured descriptions and rendered the hierarchical and functional relationships between concepts. Limitations were also observed: occasional non-normative synonyms and purely qualitative descriptions of quantitative relationships. Output variability, although not measured here, is a known LLM property that calls for expert review. Under the conditions tested, GPT-4 appears to be a promising semantic assistant for studying normative vocabularies, with the controlled input context supporting a traceable assessment of its capabilities and gaps. These observations also suggest future directions, which were not tested here, such as AI-assisted teaching, standardization, and terminological interoperability.

candidates.title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.

candidates.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.

candidates.title: Learning Complementary Agent Groups via Task Hypergraphs for Next-POI Recommendation with Missing Modalities
candidates.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation uses visit histories and POI content, but text and images are often missing. Large language model agents have been applied to recommender systems for preference modeling and evidence acquisition. The challenge is to select agents that can jointly analyze the available evidence for each request. We propose \textsc{CATH} (\emph{Complementary Agents via Task Hypergraphs}), which learns to select agent groups for tasks such as comparing candidates or analyzing a POI with missing content. Agents with distinct processing roles are the task hypergraph nodes; each hyperedge connects the selected group and records its analysis goal and target POIs. The policy selects members conditioned on the request, task, and agents already selected. During execution, members share candidate-linked results that guide their subsequent operations. Completed tasks update candidate states and agent memories within the request. A shared ranking head converts candidate states into corrections to a fixed base ranking. Supervised ranking trains the executor, followed by policy optimization that accounts for computation cost. Experiments under natural missingness on Gowalla-CA, Foursquare-NYC, and Foursquare-TKY show 8.4--9.1\% relative NDCG@20 gains over HyperAgent4POI, the strongest prior baseline evaluated. Additional analyses compare group-selection and execution designs, test ranking under additional masking, and characterize quality--cost tradeoffs.

candidates.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.

candidates.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
candidates.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Compression for Autoregressive Text Generation: Methods, Evaluation, and Deployment Trade-Offs
candidates.abstract: Compression changes both the information retained by a large language model and the resources required to complete a request. This narrative review examines quantization, pruning and sparsity, knowledge distillation, low-rank factorization, and token, context, and key–value cache compression for autoregressive text generation, principally with decoder-only LLMs. Its central contribution is a synthesis of changes relative to each study’s baseline, connecting compression mechanisms to capability and deployment choices. Four numerical tables distinguish quality changes at stated compression budgets, distillation gains over same-size students, and paired or independent deployment measurements. Reporting is appraised by source identity, comparison conditions, measurement scope, artefacts, and uncertainty. The reviewed cases illustrate how capacity constraints change the feasible precision choices, how allocating a shared budget changes different task scores, and how compact-model construction and request compression address complementary resource demands. A deployment-validation sequence turns these findings into candidate checks for a target workload. Remaining questions concern transfer across capabilities, delayed use of compressed information, interactions between compression stages, and complete-task cost, including agent interactions.

candidates.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.

candidates.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

candidates.title: Beyond Retrieval: Bidirectional Neuro-Symbolic Validation for Reliable Graph-RAG
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and its graph-based extensions improve factual grounding in LLMs but do not guarantee logical consistency when responses must satisfy explicit domain constraints. We propose a bidirectional neuro-symbolic validation framework for Graph-RAG that combines First-Order Logic reasoning over a domain knowledge graph with an Annotated Datalog engine built on PyReason, propagating confidence bounds across inferred facts. A bidirectional mechanism supports symbolic enrichment, post-hoc validation with corrective rewriting, and direct symbolic execution. In a Brazilian public university advisory benchmark, the framework achieves strict accuracy of 84.2% and weighted accuracy of 87.7% (with partial-credit weighting), an 87% reduction in factual errors relative to LLM-only; a backend-sensitivity study with gemma4:12b preserves the baseline ordering with no answer labeled incorrect (0/57).

candidates.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

candidates.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.

candidates.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
candidates.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

candidates.title: Autonomous intelligence for mining productivity: a multi-agent AI approach to operational value creation
candidates.abstract: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.

candidates.title: A Fisher-Geometric View of Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
candidates.abstract: Consolidating specialized foundation models into a unified generalist is a central goal of post-training. Two approaches are in common use: model merging, which is fast but treated as a heuristic, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which matches distributions but demands heavy rollout compute and suffers from cross-task gradient conflict. We show that the two are one objective seen at different orders. Within a shared basin of homologous specialists, the multi-teacher on-policy distillation objective is, to second order, exactly the Fisher-merging objective. Its minimizer is therefore the Fisher merge, a classic model-merging method given by a closed-form combination of the specialists, so merging is optimal, to second order, as a closed-form stage of distillation. Building on this identification, we propose Residual-Governed Branch-and-Merge(RGBM), a two-phase consolidation procedure. Concretely, a full-parameter Fisher merge is intractable on foundation models, so Phase~1 restricts the merge to the task-vector subspace. Extending tangent-space analyses of merging, we show that the same coefficients that mix task vectors also mix implicit rewards, which lets a residual program on unlabelled prompts solve for them. The program minimizes the worst per-domain residual and reports its energy-normalized values as the domain residual spectrum. Phase~2 lets this spectrum govern what may be added: RGBM passivates domains with low normalized residuals, trains isolated branches only for domains above the spectral gap, and writes back the admitted updates with calibrated shrinkage. On two open-source consolidation suites, the Phase~1 merge alone matches or outperforms fully trained multi-teacher distillation, and RGBM improves on it further with zero extra joint-training steps, whereas every un-gated write-back, including continued joint distillation from the merge, falls below it.

candidates.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
candidates.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.

candidates.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
candidates.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

candidates.title: EchoMed Agent: A Foundation Model–Based Agentic Framework for Echocardiographic Left Ventricular Segmentation and Functional Assessment

candidates.title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine
candidates.abstract: Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. candidates.title: When Safety Fails Collectively: Robust Alignment Against Harmful Fine-Tuning via Joint Weight Perturbations

We identify a collective failure pattern: disjoint parts of a harmful perturbation have limited effects in isolation, but their joint application increases the model's harmfulness beyond the sum of their individual effects. Guided by this observation, we propose Joint Weight Perturbations (JWP), an alignment-stage defense that masks different parts of a harmful perturbation estimated from the current model and trains the model to respond safely in the resulting states. This exposes the model to different combinations of harmful perturbations and reduces its sensitivity to their accumulation during subsequent harmful fine-tuning. Experiments across downstream tasks and model families show that JWP offers stronger resistance to harmful fine-tuning than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.

candidates.title: Think, Compress, Answer: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Grounding via Reasoning Compression

TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. candidates.title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code

candidates.title: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
candidates.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often weakens their previously aligned safety behavior, creating an inherent trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this issue by identifying safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space. However, safety-related information is often distributed across many directions in this space, causing downstream updates to overwrite parameters that encode safety behavior. We propose WSR-Tune, a Weight Space Reparameterization-based fine-tuning framework that preserves safety during downstream adaptation. Our approach constructs a safety-conditioned basis and reparameterizes the weight matrices such that safety-relevant information becomes concentrated in a small subset of directions. We then identify safety-critical directions and freeze them in the reparameterized space, while updating the remaining complementary directions for downstream adaptation. By explicitly structuring the parameter space to disentangle safety and task information, our method reduces interference between objectives and enables simultaneous preservation of safety and improvement in downstream performance. Experimental results show that our method achieves a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable LLM fine-tuning.
